It started raining on a Tuesday in May, at four in the afternoon, and didn't stop for three days. It wasn't the light rain of the Florentine spring, the kind that washes the streets and makes the stones shine. It was heavy, vertical, furious rain, which the newspapers immediately called a "water bomb" and which in six hours dropped on Florence the amount of rain that usually falls in two months. On Wednesday morning the Arno, which until the day before had been a lazy green river, the colour of olives, had turned brown, swollen, very fast. It was dragging branches, tree trunks, plastic drums, even an overturned boat. From the bridges, people watched it in silence. Nobody said it aloud, but everyone was thinking the same thing: 1966.

At eleven civil protection declared a red alert for the whole Arno basin, until Thursday evening. The same message arrived on every Florentine's phone, with a shrill ringtone nobody had ever heard before: "Red alert for hydraulic risk. The public is asked not to go near embankments and underpasses, to avoid going out unless strictly necessary and not to stay in basements." The schools were closed in order to keep the children at home. The museums moved works from the underground stores to the upper floors. On the riverside roads the police put up barriers to stop onlookers from leaning over the river. Florence, for the first time in many years, seemed to be holding its breath.

Valeria Conti arrived in via Maggio at midday, soaked to the skin, in a yellow civil protection raincoat and with a list in her hand. As neighbourhood councillor, she had been entrusted with the Oltrarno emergency plan: thirty-two families living on the ground floor near the river, fourteen craft workshops, two restoration workshops, a nursery school. The first workshop on the list was the Ernesto cooperative's. She came in without knocking. Matei and Chiara were standing in front of the six paintings leaning against the walls of the ground floor, with the faces of people doing a difficult sum. "The plan provides for moving all the works off the ground floor," said Valeria, pushing back her hood, "to put them in a safe place. Have you got somewhere higher up?"

Matei looked at the marble plaque on the wall opposite, on the other side of the street, the one marking the water level of 4 November 1966: two and a half metres from the ground. He had looked at it every morning for years, but that day it seemed higher than usual. "Our flat," he said. "The first floor. It's above the plaque." Chiara was already phoning Karl and Pietro. In twenty minutes they both arrived, in rubber boots and with serious faces. Pietro had left home even though the schools had been closed precisely to prevent kids from wandering around, and Graziella, when she saw him pass in front of the trattoria, shouted something after him that couldn't be made out because of the rain. But it was clear it wasn't a reproach. It was encouragement.

Moving six old paintings up a narrow staircase, in the rain, is not like moving six pieces of furniture. Each painting had to be wrapped in a plastic sheet to prevent the humidity from reaching it, carried by two people, always kept upright, never tilted, never put down on the floor. Chiara directed the operations like a general. Karl and Matei carried. Pietro opened the doors, checked the steps, counted aloud. Giulia, on the first floor, cleared the walls of the living room and of Viola's room, taking down photos, drawings, shelves, in order to make space. Viola, who was almost five and considered the whole business a wonderful game, helped by moving her cuddly toys from one room to another, "to put them in a safe place too".

The last painting was the most delicate: a small fifteenth-century panel, with a thin crack near the Madonna's face, the same one Karl had examined on the day of his interview. Chiara wanted to carry it herself. She climbed the stairs slowly, one step at a time, with the panel held against her chest like a newborn baby, while Pietro held the door and Karl followed her with his arms outstretched, ready to catch it if it slipped. When she laid it on Viola's bed, between a teddy bear and a giraffe, everyone sighed with relief. Viola looked at the Madonna, then at the bear, then at the Madonna again. "Is she sleeping with me now?" she asked. Chiara laughed for the first time all day. "Only tonight," she said. "Tomorrow she goes back downstairs."

Then Valeria went to the families on the ground floor, and Pietro, who had finished with the paintings, followed her without asking permission. They knocked on thirty-two doors. In some houses they were welcomed with gratitude. In others with suspicion. An old gentleman in via dei Serragli didn't want to leave his home for any reason: he said that in 1966 he had stayed and that he would stay this time too. Valeria talked to him for twenty minutes, patiently, without raising her voice. In the end it was Pietro who convinced him, with a single question: "But in 1966 you were twenty. Now you're eighty-two. Who would carry you up onto the roof this time?" The old man looked at him for a long time, then took his jacket. He went to sleep at his daughter's, in Bellosguardo, on the hill. Before leaving, he shook Pietro's hand.

The only person Valeria didn't even try to convince was Graziella. The trattoria was on the ground floor, fifty metres from the river, exactly under the plaque. But when Valeria went in, Graziella had already lit all the burners. Four big pots were boiling on the stove: ribollita, pasta and beans, broth, sauce. On the counter there were a hundred sandwiches wrapped in paper. "In 1966 I was twelve," said Graziella without turning round, stirring the ribollita. "My mother stayed here three days cooking for the angels of the mud, with the water up to her knees. I carried the plates. I'm not leaving, Valeria. Tonight someone will be working on the embankments, and someone will have to feed them." Valeria said nothing. She took off her raincoat, picked up an apron and started cutting the bread.

Meanwhile, in the empty workshop, Karl phoned don Paolo. The Madonna from the church of San Leonardo was due to arrive in Florence the following Monday, for the last analyses before the open worksite, and Karl wanted to know whether everything was all right in the countryside. Don Paolo answered on the fifth ring, with his usual calm voice. "My son," he said, "the church is on top of a hill. The water doesn't get here. Only the wind does." Then he added that, to prevent the Madonna from running needless risks, he would prefer to postpone the journey by a week. "May I suggest," he said, with a formula that made Karl smile, "that we leave her where she is until the river has calmed down. She has waited seven hundred years. She can wait seven days." Before hanging up, he promised to light a candle for Florence that evening. Just one, he specified. So as not to yellow the varnish.

At about six Efisio arrived, Davide's grandfather, with Davide and an old army rucksack on his back. He was over eighty, but he walked through the rain like a boy. In the rucksack there were a torch, a rope, a pair of boots and a small folding shovel. "Is it the same one from 1966?" asked Pietro. Efisio laughed. "I lost that one in the mud at Santa Croce," he said. "I bought this one in 1967, just in case. I've never used it. Let's hope I don't use it this time either." He sat down at the table by the window, the one from which you could see the plaque, and didn't move all night. Davide sat beside him, with his sketchbook, and began to draw him, while outside the rain beat on the windows like a thousand impatient fingers.

That evening someone nobody knew came into the trattoria: Professor Marta Innocenti, a hydraulic engineer at the University of Florence, who worked for civil protection and had spent the day checking the river gauges along the river. She was a woman of fifty, with short wet hair and a tablet sealed in a plastic bag. She came in for a coffee and left three hours later, because Pietro asked her so many questions that she couldn't get away. Over a bowl of ribollita, she explained to everyone why, in her opinion, the Arno would not overflow that night. "After 1966 we learned a lot," she said. "We built the Bilancino dam, on the Sieve, in order to hold back the water upstream. And in recent years the retention basins."

Pietro asked what retention basins were. The professor took a paper napkin and drew a river, with some rectangles at the sides. "They're large fields near the river, surrounded by low embankments," she explained. "When the river rises too much, a passage opens and the water flows into the fields, instead of reaching the city. The basins serve to stop the river from overflowing where there are houses. It follows that, if we sacrifice a bit of countryside, we save Florence." Efisio, from his table, nodded slowly. "In 1966 there was none of this," he said. "The river came at night and nobody knew anything. There were no phones that ring. We realised when the water came in through the doors." The professor looked at him with respect. "It's precisely to prevent it happening again," she said, "that we do what we do."

But then she said something that made the trattoria fall silent. "The problem," she explained, "is that the works we've built were designed for twentieth-century rainfall. But the climate is changing. Water bombs like today's, thirty years ago, happened once every fifty years. Now they happen almost every year, somewhere in Italy. As an effect of global warming, warmer air holds more water vapour, and when it rains, it all comes down at once." She paused. "And then in summer there's the opposite problem: drought. Last year, in August, the Arno was so low you could walk across it near Pisa. Too much water or too little. That's what climate change is: not hotter, but more extreme."

Around midnight the rain doubled. The civil protection workers and the volunteers working on the embankments with sandbags began arriving at the trattoria in groups of three or four, soaked to the bone, their hands red with cold. Graziella fed everyone, without asking for anything: ribollita, sandwiches, hot coffee, a slice of cake. Valeria waited at the tables. Karl washed the dishes. Matei and Giulia, after putting Viola to bed between the cuddly toys and the fifteenth-century Madonna, came down to lend a hand. Bellini, whom the cardiologist had sent to bed at nine, arrived at half past eleven with his stick and an enormous umbrella, and sat down next to Efisio. "Two old men at the window," he said. "In 1966 I was in my grandfather's arms. This time it's my turn to watch."

At two in the morning Professor Innocenti's phone vibrated. She read the message, then stood up, and the whole trattoria turned towards her. "The Uffizi gauge," she said. "The level has stopped rising. The Figline basins have filled up, the dam has held back the rest. The peak has passed. We're five metres below the parapet." For a second nobody said anything. Then a volunteer in orange overalls began to applaud, and after him all the others. Efisio didn't applaud. He stayed seated, looking at the plaque on the other side of the street, and Davide saw that his eyes were full of tears. The old man took off his hat. "This time we made it," he said quietly. "Without a shovel."

Among the volunteers in the trattoria that night there was a group of university students, who had come in a minibus from Pisa and Siena as soon as they heard about the alert. One of them, a twenty-year-old girl in orange overalls with her wet hair tied in a ponytail, came over to Efisio's table. She had heard Sardinian being spoken. She was from Nuoro, she said, like him. Efisio looked at her as you look at a ghost, then took her hand. They talked in Sardinian for half an hour, and nobody understood a word, but everyone understood everything. At the end the girl took out of her rucksack a book with a cover drawn by Davide: it was "Il fango e la Madonna", Bellini's book. She asked Efisio to sign it. He wrote a single sentence, in Sardinian, and then translated it for the others: "To the angels of the water, from an angel of the mud. You arrived in time."

On Thursday morning it stopped raining. The sky over Florence was a blue so clean it looked washed, and the Arno, still brown and fast, flowed under the bridges without touching them. In via Maggio, Chiara, Karl, Matei and Pietro carried the six paintings back down, one at a time, with the same care with which they had carried them up. The last to come down was the fifteenth-century Madonna, who had slept in Viola's bed. Viola waved goodbye to her from the bedroom door. "Bye, Madonna," she said. "Come back when it rains." Chiara checked the panel with a magnifying glass. The crack hadn't widened by a millimetre. "Thanks to the plastic sheet," she said. "And thanks to the fact that we avoided tilting it. And thanks to the teddy bear, I imagine."

That afternoon, in the neighbourhood council chamber, Valeria called an extraordinary meeting. Present were the councillors, Professor Innocenti, the head of the neighbourhood's civil protection and, by special invitation, Efisio, Graziella and Pietro. Valeria spoke for ten minutes. She said the night just gone had shown two things. First: that the emergency plan worked. Second: that it worked thanks to people, not just dams. "I propose," she said, "to create a neighbourhood network for emergencies, in order to make sure that nobody, in the Oltrarno, is left alone during an alert. Every building will have a contact person. Every elderly person living alone will have a neighbour who knocks on their door. And every workshop will have a plan to put its most precious things in a safe place."

The proposal was approved unanimously. The lawyer Bardi asked for the floor only to say that, for once, he didn't need to add "prudently", because the proposal was itself a form of prudence. Then Professor Innocenti asked if she could say something. She explained that she had been studying rivers for twenty years, and had written dozens of scientific articles on floods. "But last night," she said, "I learned something that isn't in any article. A fourteen-year-old boy persuaded an eighty-two-year-old man to leave his home with a single question. And a lady of over seventy fed a hundred volunteers without asking for anything. Dams hold back water. But it's people who hold a city together."

The following week, at school, Pietro and Davide proposed an end-of-year project to their science teacher. It would be called "The river we forgot", and would have three parts. The first, about 1966, with interviews with Efisio, Graziella and the old gentleman from via dei Serragli. The second, about science, with Professor Innocenti, who had agreed to come to class to explain retention basins and climate change. The third, about the future, with a question for every classmate: "What will you do to prevent it happening again?" The answers were of every kind. Bianca wrote that she would become a hydraulic engineer. Sara wrote that she would use the car less. One boy wrote only: "I'll learn to make ribollita."

The drawing Davide had made that night became the cover of the project. It showed two old men sitting at the trattoria window, one with a hat and one with a stick, watching the rain. Behind them, blurred, a woman stirring a pot, a woman cutting bread, a boy washing dishes. Outside the window, on the wall opposite, the 1966 plaque. And above the plaque, very small, drawn in pencil, a new line, much lower, with a date: the May night when the river had stopped. Underneath, Davide had written the title in his crooked handwriting: "This time without a shovel." Efisio, when he saw it, asked for a copy. He hung it in his kitchen, next to the photo of his 1966 shovel, the one he had never found again.

That evening Pietro wrote in the black notebook, under the date. He copied the alert message that had arrived on the phones, word for word, because he thought that one day someone would want to read it, as he read Ernesto's diary of 1966. Then he wrote: "In 1966 the river came at night and nobody knew. This year it came at night and everyone knew. The difference isn't the river. It's that someone, after 1966, asked themselves questions. Why did it happen? How can we prevent it happening again? The dams are the answers to those questions." He reread it, then added a line, thinking of Professor Innocenti and the drought at Pisa: "Now it's our turn to ask the new questions. Because the river changes, and the questions must change too."
